newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- US factory output unchanged in April.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- US factory output unchanged in April.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Federal Reserve said industrial production was unchanged in April, while capacity utilization stood at 83.4 percent in the month.
Economists had expected factory output to rise 0.2 percent and capacity use to print 84.1 percent.

ASTRID ADOLFSON, VICE PRESIDENT, MCM MONEYWATCH INC: "(The report) shows that manufacturing is still in an uptrend, but obviously not as much as it had been. It could be other factors that are holding it down.
Adolfson continued: "It's too early to detect a trend here. (But) the data ... are indicating that there is still very good momentum out there. I think the (Federal Reserve) will look through this.
"We still say the Fed will tighten by 25 basis points (at the May 20 Federal Open Market Committee meeting)."

SUZANNE RIZZO, ECONOMIST, MFR INC: "The number looks trendlike. This is not particularly the indicator the Fed was looking at (in making policy decisions); they're more worried about labor tightness."

RICHARD BERNER, EXECUTIVE VICE PRESIDENT AND CHIEF ECONOMIST, MELLON BANK CORP: "(The data) probably understate strength ... in the manufacturing sector and in the economy as a whole. We had a sharp decline in the motor vehicle area; most of that was due to strikes at Chrysler and General Motors. In addition, floods and other weather-related disturbances probably affected these data to some extent. While we've got a flat number for April, we'll probably see more strength as we move forward in the second quarter."
RAPHAEL MARRONE, MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL: "It's below our forecast ... but a lot of this is strike related too, so, we should have a rebound next month.

"The market should look beyond this number which is distorted by strike ... The GM people are still off, so it may not rebound as strongly but we should get a pretty strong reading in (the National Association of Purchasing Management report) once we get that out in a couple of weeks."

CHARLES LIEBERMAN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CHASE SECURITIES INC: "The industrial production number was flat, with the auto sector weak, as expected because of the strikes. Ex-autos, industrial production was up 0.3 percent. Auto assemblies slowed to a 5.7 million rate in April from 6.2 million in March and truck assemblies slowed to a 5.2 million rate in April versus 6.0 million in March.
"There was some easing in capacity utilization partly because of the downward revision to industrial production in March to 0.6 percent from the 0.9 percent rise first reported.

Lieberman continued: "The numbers are probably consistent with a picture of moderate, ongoing gains in industrial activity. April was flat due to the auto strikes, so that production will bounce back.
"These data will not be a signifciant factor in Federal Reserve thinking on monetary policy," he added.

MARILYN SCHAJA, MONEY MARKET ECONOMIST, DONALDSON, LUFKIN AND JENRETTE SECURITIES CORP: "Overall, not the same story as retail sales, but similar in that we're seeing a slowdown in March and April ... looks like a little bit less manufacturing activity is taking place. And capacity use figures are fitting with that. Those numbers were revised downwards so there is less constraint there."
